From an aviation combustion perspective, LNG is an emission-reducing alternative to jet fuels due to its lower CO and soot emissions. Additionally, there are many technical challenges associated with aircraft modifications, fuel handling, fuel storage, and airport and national infrastructure. 5 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 1.1.4 Liquefied Ethane Ethane (C H ) is a naturally occurring gas component derived primarily from natural gas 2 6 processing facilities by demethanization and fractionation. Ethane is a cryogenic liquid at −89°C (184 K) and possesses an energy density comparable to that of LNG (see Figure 4)—making it a very good energy carrier. Ethane production depends greatly on natural gas processing steps such as dehydration, contaminant removal, and deep fractionation, as shown in Figure 5. Plants first fractionate off methane and other light gases before passing mixed natural gas liquids through deethanizers, depropanizers, and debutanizers to separate ethane, propane, butanes, and natural gasoline. Although this process is very well established, the associated downstream logistic network for large-scale transport of ethane is still developing. Figure 5. Natural gas processing. Source: EIA (2014a) Unlike LNG, LE is seldom used as a propulsion fuel with few applications in rocket engines and marine LE carriers. The main applications are in the petrochemical industry for the production of ethene (ethylene) and acetic acid, and for some refrigeration processes. Of these, the most significant and well-established commercial application of ethane currently is production of ethylene, and demand is expected to remain strong for many years (EIA 2025k). However, the global supply chain infrastructure to support transport of ethane, including terminals, specialized vessels, and associated logistics, is much less well developed compared with LNG. As a result, there is comparatively little technical and operational research published that specifically considers the problems of storing and carrying LE in aviation applications. Ethane exhibits lower and wider flammability limits than LNG, meaning it can ignite over a broader range of concentrations, as seen in Figure 6.
